title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text: # Runbook: Deployment Rollback

title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text:
## Use When
- Errors begin shortly after a deployment event.
- Failures map to changed code paths or configuration.
- No wider dependency or database outage explains the symptoms.

title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text:
## Triage
1. Find the latest deployment for the affected service.
2. Compare error onset with deployment timestamp.
3. Check whether a feature flag can disable the risky behavior.
4. Review whether migrations are backward compatible before rolling back.

title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text:
## Decision Criteria
- Roll back when the release timing, changed code path, and error signature all point to the new version.
- Prefer feature flag disablement when it fully avoids the failing behavior and has lower blast radius.

title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text:
- Avoid rollback when schema changes are forward-only or the old version cannot read current data.
- Roll forward with a patch when rollback risk is higher than the current incident risk.

title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text:
## Remediation
- Prefer feature flag disablement when it fully avoids the failing path.
- Roll back the service when the new version is strongly correlated with the incident.
- Avoid rollback if it would run old code against an incompatible schema.

title: Runbook: Deployment Rollback
text:
## Verification
Error rate should fall below the configured incident threshold within one or two traffic windows. Confirm latency also returns toward its normal range and that no new schema, queue, or compatibility errors appear after the rollback.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text: # Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text:
## Symptoms
- p95 latency rises across multiple services.
- Logs include `connection acquisition timeout`, `pool exhausted`, or `too many clients`.
- Database CPU may be normal while app request queues grow.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text:
## Triage
1. Check whether the issue affects one service or all services.
2. Compare database pool usage, active connections, and slow query count.
3. Look for a recent deployment that changed connection pool size or transaction handling.
4. Confirm whether long-running transactions are holding connections.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text:
## Decision Criteria
- Treat as app pool exhaustion when app pool usage is saturated but PostgreSQL still has available connections.
- Treat as too many connections when PostgreSQL rejects new sessions before queries run.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text:
- Treat as slow query or lock contention when connections are available but query or lock wait time is elevated.
- Choose rollback only when the timing matches a deployment that changed pool size, worker count, or transaction scope.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text:
## Remediation
- Restart the affected service only if leaked connections are suspected and requests are failing.
- Roll back the latest deployment if pool configuration or transaction scope changed.
- Temporarily reduce worker concurrency if the database is saturated.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text: - Do not increase pool size until database max connections and downstream capacity are confirmed.

title: Runbook: Database Connection Exhaustion
text:
## Verification
Latency should fall below threshold, connection acquisition errors should stop, and active connection count should return to normal.

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text: # Runbook: Memory Leak

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text:
## Symptoms
- Memory usage rises steadily over time.
- Latency increases after sustained traffic.
- Restarts temporarily fix the problem, then memory rises again.

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text:
## Triage
1. Compare memory growth with traffic volume and deployment events.
2. Look for repeated large payload processing, cache growth, or unbounded lists.
3. Check whether one pod or all pods are affected.
4. Distinguish memory leak from temporary spike during batch work.

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text:
## Decision Criteria
- Treat as memory leak when memory rises steadily and does not return to baseline after traffic drops.
- Treat as traffic spike when memory and latency normalize after load returns to baseline.

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text:
- Restart only affected instances when recovery is urgent and enough diagnostic evidence has been captured.
- Roll back or disable a feature when the memory slope began after a release or feature flag change.

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text:
## Remediation
- Restart only the affected instances to restore service while preserving evidence.
- Roll back if the leak began after a deployment.
- Disable the feature path if a flag controls the allocation-heavy behavior.
- Capture heap or object statistics before broad restarts when possible.

title: Runbook: Memory Leak
text:
## Verification
Memory usage should stabilize below the configured threshold, the memory growth slope should flatten, restarts should stop, and p95 latency should return toward its normal range.

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text: # Runbook: External Dependency Failure

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text:
## Symptoms
- One service reports timeouts or 5xx responses from a downstream provider.
- Internal database and CPU metrics remain healthy.
- Retries increase request latency and may amplify load.

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text:
## Triage
1. Identify the failing dependency and affected endpoint.
2. Check timeout rate, retry count, and circuit breaker state.
3. Compare provider errors with internal deployment events.
4. Confirm whether fallback or degraded mode is available.

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text:
## Decision Criteria
- Treat as external provider failure when internal CPU, database, and deployment signals are clean.
- Treat as internal client/config failure when errors begin immediately after a deployment or timeout change.
- Prefer degraded mode when user impact can be reduced without corrupting state.

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text: - Reduce retries when retry volume is increasing queues or making downstream saturation worse.

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text:
## Remediation
- Enable circuit breaker or degraded mode when supported.
- Reduce retry attempts if retries are causing queue buildup.
- Roll back only when the dependency failure starts immediately after a client/config deployment.
- Escalate to the provider when internal metrics are clean.

title: Runbook: External Dependency Failure
text:
## Verification
Timeout rate should decrease, queues should drain, and successful degraded responses should replace hard failures. If normal operation is restored, confirm dependency calls succeed without excessive retries before disabling the circuit breaker or degraded mode.

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text: # Runbook: Payment Service Degradation

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text:
## Symptoms
- Checkout failures or pending payments rise.
- Payment-service logs include gateway timeout, idempotency conflict, or provider 5xx.
- Order service may show downstream payment errors while user service remains healthy.

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text:
## Triage
1. Check payment error rate and gateway timeout rate.
2. Compare failures by provider, region, and payment method.
3. Inspect recent payment-service deployment or gateway config changes.
4. Confirm whether idempotency keys are being reused correctly.

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text:
## Decision Criteria
- Treat as provider degradation when gateway timeout or provider 5xx rises without a matching internal deployment.
- Treat as payment-service regression when failures begin immediately after release or config change.
- Prioritize idempotency protection when duplicate attempts or conflicts appear in logs.

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text: - Use degraded mode when authorization is unreliable but orders can safely remain pending.

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text:
## Remediation
- Enable payment degraded mode if the gateway is timing out.
- Roll back the payment-service deployment if errors started after release.
- Reduce retry fanout if duplicate attempts are creating conflicts.
- Do not manually mark payments successful without provider confirmation.

title: Runbook: Payment Service Degradation
text:
## Verification
New checkout attempts should succeed, payment gateway timeout rate should fall below the incident threshold, pending payment backlog should shrink, and duplicate charge alerts should remain at zero.

title: Database Architecture
text: # Database Architecture

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Purpose
LiveOps uses PostgreSQL as the system of record for incident history, telemetry samples, and remediation audit events. The database supports operator dashboards and gives the agent durable context about what happened, what was attempted, and whether recovery succeeded.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Core Tables
- `logs`: structured application logs from `payment-service`, `order-service`, `user-service`, and edge workers. Logs carry timestamp, service, level, message, and optional request id.
- `metrics`: sampled service metrics such as latency, error rate, memory usage, queue depth, database pool usage, and dependency timeout rate.

title: Database Architecture
text:
- `events`: deployment, feature flag, autoscaling, dependency, and remediation events. These are lower-volume facts used to explain metric changes.
- `incidents`: detected incidents with service, incident type, severity, message, status, metric value, and threshold.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Relationships
The core telemetry tables are correlated by `service`, timestamp window, and optional `request_id` rather than strict foreign keys. A single incident is usually explained by a cluster of related rows:
- `incidents` is the starting point for agent investigation and stores the detected symptom.

title: Database Architecture
text:
- `metrics` provides the numeric evidence that crossed a threshold or shows recovery.
- `logs` provides request-level or worker-level detail for the same service and time window.
- `events` explains changes around the incident, such as deployments, feature flag updates, dependency changes, restarts, and remediation attempts.

title: Database Architecture
text: For example, a database failure incident may have an `incidents` row for `api` latency, `metrics` rows for pool usage or failed connection attempts, `logs` rows with connection errors, and `events` rows showing a database restart or injected failure.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Access Pattern
The API writes telemetry through repository methods instead of direct model access. Detection jobs read recent windows of metrics and logs, then create an `incidents` row when thresholds are crossed. The agent reads incidents first, then follows related logs, metrics, and events by timestamp and service.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Query Shape
Most investigation queries filter by:
- `service`
- recent timestamp window
- incident type or metric name
- request id when a single user flow is affected

title: Database Architecture
text: Indexes should be added first on `timestamp`, `service`, and combined `service, timestamp` when data volume grows. Incident status views should prefer indexed status and timestamp predicates.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Retention
High-cardinality logs and metrics can be retained for a shorter window in production, usually 14-30 days. Incidents and remediation events should be retained longer because they train retrieval and post-incident analysis. Historical Markdown incidents in the knowledge base are curated summaries, not replacements for database records.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Failure Modes
- Database unavailable: services fail to open new connections and logs show connection refused, host unreachable, DNS failure, or database timeout errors. This should trigger broad blast-radius investigation because API, detection, telemetry writes, and incident persistence may all degrade at once.

title: Database Architecture
text: - Too many connections: PostgreSQL rejects new sessions with too many clients or remaining connection slots reserved errors. App logs may show authentication succeeded but connection creation failed before queries ran. This is different from slow queries because the database may be responsive for existing sessions.

title: Database Architecture
text: - Connection pool exhaustion: app workers wait for a pool slot and logs show connection acquisition timeouts. This can happen even when PostgreSQL still has capacity, usually because the service is holding connections too long.

title: Database Architecture
text:
- Slow queries: p95 latency rises while connections are available. Slow query logs or lock waits identify the affected table or transaction.
- Migration errors: failures correlate with a recent deployment event and schema-related exceptions such as missing columns, invalid enum values, or incompatible rollback behavior.

title: Database Architecture
text:
## Operational Notes
Keep remediation writes idempotent. If the agent retries an action after a timeout, the audit event should include the same action key or request id so duplicate attempts can be recognized later.

title: System Architecture
text: # System Architecture

title: System Architecture
text:
## Overview
LiveOps is an incident-response simulation platform. FastAPI exposes telemetry, incident, deployment, and remediation endpoints. Service modules simulate user, order, and payment behavior. Detection logic watches metrics and creates incidents. The agent investigates, diagnoses, remediates, and verifies recovery.

title: System Architecture
text:
## Main Components
- Frontend dashboard: shows active incidents, diagnosis, remediation actions, and verification results.
- API layer: accepts telemetry and exposes incident workflows.
- Services: `user-service`, `order-service`, and `payment-service` model common production dependencies.
- Detection: threshold-based incident detection over recent telemetry.

title: System Architecture
text:
- Agent: graph-based workflow for investigation, diagnosis, remediation, and verification.
- Knowledge base: runbooks, architecture notes, and historical incidents used for retrieval.

title: System Architecture
text:
## Incident Flow
Telemetry arrives through API endpoints or traffic generation scripts. Detection compares recent metrics with configured thresholds. When an incident is opened, the agent gathers logs, metrics, events, and retrieved knowledge base chunks before recommending or executing actions.

title: System Architecture
text:
## Deployment Events
Deployments are first-class events because many incidents are caused by config changes, schema drift, or new code paths. Rollback is allowed only when the suspected deployment is recent and verification can confirm user-facing recovery.

title: System Architecture
text:
## Service Boundaries
Order service owns checkout orchestration. Payment service owns provider calls, retries, idempotency keys, and payment status. User service owns profile and session lookups. Cross-service calls should include request ids so related logs can be tied together during investigation.

title: System Architecture
text:
## Reliability Priorities
The platform favors safe recovery over aggressive automation. The agent should gather enough evidence to distinguish similar failures, choose the lowest-risk remediation, and verify that error rate and latency return below threshold.

title: Service Dependencies
text: # Service Dependencies

title: Service Dependencies
text:
## Dependency Map
- Frontend depends on FastAPI API endpoints.
- API depends on PostgreSQL for telemetry and incident state.
- Order service depends on user service for account state and payment service for checkout.
- Payment service depends on the external payment gateway and database idempotency records.

title: Service Dependencies
text: - Agent depends on telemetry repositories, remediation actions, verification checks, and retrieved knowledge base chunks.

title: Service Dependencies
text:
## Critical Paths
Checkout is the most sensitive path. A normal request touches order service, user service, payment service, PostgreSQL, and the payment gateway. A failure in any part can appear as checkout latency or payment errors, so investigation must look at dependency health before selecting remediation.

title: Service Dependencies
text:
## Common Correlations
- Payment gateway timeout: payment-service timeout logs, elevated dependency timeout rate, normal database pool usage.
- Database pool exhaustion: API and service latency rise together, connection acquisition errors, normal external gateway health.

title: Service Dependencies
text:
- Bad deployment: errors begin within minutes of a deployment event and often affect one service or endpoint first.
- Memory leak: gradual memory climb followed by latency and restarts, often without a deployment exactly at onset.

title: Service Dependencies
text:
## Blast Radius
User service degradation can cause login and checkout failures. Payment service degradation can leave orders pending or rejected. Database degradation affects all services and should be treated as broad blast radius even if the first alert names one service.

title: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API
text:
# Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API

Date: 2026-04-08 
Service: api 
Severity: high
section: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API

title: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API
text:
## Summary
The API returned intermittent 500s and slow dashboard responses. All services showed some latency because API workers waited for PostgreSQL connections.

title: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API
text:
## Signals
- `db.pool.in_use` stayed at 100%.
- Logs showed `connection acquisition timeout`.
- Slow query count was low.

title: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API
text:
## Cause
A code path opened a transaction before calling downstream services and held the connection while waiting.

title: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API
text:
## Resolution
Restarted affected API workers and deployed a patch that opened transactions only around database writes.

title: Incident 002: Database Pool Exhaustion In API
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to slow query incidents, but the pool was exhausted even though queries were not slow.

title: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive
text:
# Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive

Date: 2026-06-15 
Service: order-service 
Severity: medium
section: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive

title: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive
text:
## Summary
Order-service rejected valid checkout attempts because the payment circuit breaker opened during a brief provider blip and stayed open too long.

title: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive
text:
## Signals
- Payment gateway recovered within 3 minutes.
- Order-service continued returning fallback errors for 21 minutes.
- Circuit breaker logs showed an elevated cool-down interval.

title: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive
text:
## Cause
A config change increased circuit breaker cool-down to 30 minutes.

title: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive
text:
## Resolution
Restored cool-down to 2 minutes and manually half-opened the breaker.

title: Incident 012: Dependency Circuit Breaker Too Sensitive
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to provider outages, but failure continued after provider recovery.

title: Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression
text:
# Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression

Date: 2026-05-03 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: high

title: Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression
text:
## Summary
Checkout failures rose immediately after a payment-service deploy. Logs showed gateway timeout messages, but provider status was clean.

title: Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression
text:
## Signals
- Errors began 4 minutes after deploy `payment-service:2026.05.03.2`.
- Timeout budget changed from 2500ms to 700ms.
- Retries increased queue depth.

title: Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression
text:
## Cause
The new payment client config used a timeout lower than normal gateway p95.

title: Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression
text:
## Resolution
Rolled back payment-service and drained the retry queue.

title: Incident 006: Payment Client Config Regression
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to provider timeout incidents, but the deployment timestamp and changed timeout setting identify this as internal.

title: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike
text:
# Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike

Date: 2026-07-12 
Service: api 
Severity: medium
section: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike

title: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike
text:
## Summary
API latency rose during a traffic spike. Database, payment provider, and service error rates stayed healthy.

title: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike
text:
## Signals
- Request rate doubled in 9 minutes.
- CPU rose above 88% on all API workers.
- Queue depth increased without dependency errors.

title: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike
text:
## Cause
Autoscaling lagged behind legitimate traffic.

title: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike
text:
## Resolution
Increased API worker replicas and tuned the autoscaling threshold.

title: Incident 016: API Worker Saturation From Traffic Spike
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Can resemble database slowness, but dependency metrics were clean and CPU saturation led the incident.

title: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering
text:
# Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering

Date: 2026-05-11 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: medium
section: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering

title: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering
text:
## Summary
Payment-service memory climbed for two hours after receipt traffic increased. Latency rose, then two pods restarted.

title: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering
text:
## Signals
- `process.memory.rss` grew from 420MB to 1.8GB.
- Error rate stayed low until restarts.
- Heap samples pointed to cached receipt templates.

title: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering
text:
## Cause
Receipt rendering cached per-user templates without eviction.

title: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering
text:
## Resolution
Disabled rich receipt rendering with a feature flag and restarted the two largest pods.

title: Incident 007: Memory Leak In Receipt Rendering
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to general latency incidents, but gradual memory slope and restart recovery indicate leak.

title: Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog
text:
# Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog

Date: 2026-07-18 
Service: order-service 
Severity: high

title: Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog
text:
## Summary
Orders were accepted but status updates lagged. Payment succeeded, yet dashboard showed orders pending for several minutes.

title: Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog
text:
## Signals
- Queue depth increased from 300 to 19,000.
- Payment success rate remained normal.
- Worker logs showed deserialization errors on one event type.

title: Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog
text:
## Cause
A producer deployment added a field that older queue consumers did not tolerate.

title: Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog
text:
## Resolution
Rolled forward the consumer compatibility fix and replayed failed messages.

title: Incident 017: Order Event Queue Backlog
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to payment pending incidents, but provider success and queue backlog identify async processing failure.

title: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release
text:
# Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release

Date: 2026-04-14 
Service: order-service 
Severity: medium
section: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release

title: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release
text:
## Summary
Order-service latency increased gradually after a release that added checkout recommendation payloads. The service recovered after pod restarts, then memory began climbing again.

title: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release
text:
## Signals
- Memory grew from 500MB to 1.6GB over 90 minutes.
- p95 latency rose after memory exceeded 1.2GB.
- Error rate stayed below high severity threshold.

title: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release
text:
## Cause
Recommendation payloads were appended to an in-process list for debugging and never cleared.

title: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release
text:
## Resolution
Disabled recommendation debugging and rolled forward a patch that removed the retained list.

title: Incident 003: Order Service Memory Growth After Release
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to traffic saturation because latency rose under load, but memory slope was the leading indicator.

title: Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill
text:
# Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill

Date: 2026-06-22 
Service: api 
Severity: high

title: Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill
text:
## Summary
Telemetry writes slowed and incident creation lagged. Database pool was not exhausted, but writes waited behind a backfill transaction.

title: Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill
text:
## Signals
- Lock wait time increased.
- Active connections stayed moderate.
- A maintenance event started 12 minutes before the alert.

title: Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill
text:
## Cause
A backfill updated incidents in one large transaction and blocked newer writes.

title: Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill
text:
## Resolution
Canceled the backfill and reran it in small batches.

title: Incident 013: Database Lock From Backfill
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to slow query and pool exhaustion symptoms, but lock waits and maintenance event point to transaction blocking.

title: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard
text:
# Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard

Date: 2026-05-17 
Service: api 
Severity: medium
section: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard

title: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard
text:
## Summary
The incident dashboard became slow while service APIs remained mostly healthy. Database connections were available, but a status filter query scanned the full incidents table.

title: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard
text:
## Signals
- `api.dashboard.p95` exceeded 3s.
- Slow query logs showed `SELECT ... FROM incidents WHERE status`.
- Pool usage peaked at 62%, not exhausted.

title: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard
text:
## Cause
Missing index on incident status and timestamp after incident volume increased.

title: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard
text:
## Resolution
Added an index and changed dashboard query ordering.

title: Incident 008: Slow Query On Incident Dashboard
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Looks similar to pool exhaustion, but active connections were not saturated.

title: Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout
text:
# Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout

Date: 2026-07-26 
Service: user-service 
Severity: medium

title: Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout
text:
## Summary
Profile lookups intermittently timed out, causing checkout preflight failures. Database metrics were normal for core tables.

title: Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout
text:
## Signals
- Timeout logs named the preferences dependency.
- Login was mostly healthy; checkout preflight was affected.
- Error spikes matched calls that requested marketing preferences.

title: Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout
text:
## Cause
The optional preferences service degraded and user-service treated it as required.

title: Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout
text:
## Resolution
Enabled fallback preferences and lowered timeout from 2s to 300ms.

title: Incident 018: User Service Dependency Timeout
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to user-service database issues, but only optional preference lookups failed.

title: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak
text:
# Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak

Date: 2026-05-24 
Service: user-service 
Severity: high
section: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak

title: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak
text:
## Summary
Login latency rose during a promotion. Memory climbed on all user-service pods and sessions started timing out.

title: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak
text:
## Signals
- Memory increased in proportion to login volume.
- No recent deployment in the first hour of the incident.
- Restarting one pod fixed that pod temporarily.

title: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak
text:
## Cause
An unbounded in-memory session cache retained expired sessions during high traffic.

title: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak
text:
## Resolution
Restarted affected pods in batches and lowered cache TTL through config.

title: Incident 009: User Service Session Cache Leak
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to payment-service memory leak, but no receipt code or payment path was involved.

title: Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure
text:
# Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure

Date: 2026-08-03 
Service: api 
Severity: high

title: Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure
text:
## Summary
After credential rotation, some API pods failed database authentication while older pods stayed healthy.

title: Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure
text:
## Signals
- Logs showed `password authentication failed`.
- Errors affected only newly restarted pods.
- Database connection count dropped instead of rising.

title: Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure
text:
## Cause
Secret rollout updated the database password but not every deployment environment variable.

title: Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure
text:
## Resolution
Redeployed API pods with the corrected secret reference.

title: Incident 019: Database Credential Rotation Failure
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Different from pool exhaustion: connections failed at authentication rather than waiting for available pool slots.

title: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion
text:
# Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion

Date: 2026-04-21 
Service: order-service 
Severity: high
section: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion

title: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion
text:
## Summary
Checkout p95 rose above 2.8s and order submissions timed out. Payment gateway health was normal. Logs showed database connection acquisition timeouts from order-service workers.

title: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion
text:
## Signals
- `db.pool.in_use` stayed above 95%.
- `order.checkout.p95` rose steadily for 18 minutes.
- No provider 5xx increase.

title: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion
text:
## Cause
A release increased worker concurrency without increasing transaction discipline. Connections were held during payment-service calls.

title: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion
text:
## Resolution
Rolled back order-service and restarted saturated workers. Latency returned to normal within 8 minutes.

title: Incident 004: Checkout Latency From Connection Pool Exhaustion
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to slow database incidents, but the key clue was pool acquisition timeout rather than query duration.

title: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser
text:
# Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser

Date: 2026-06-29 
Service: api 
Severity: medium
section: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser

title: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser
text:
## Summary
Detection stopped creating incidents for payment errors because the metrics parser dropped percentage units after a deployment.

title: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser
text:
## Signals
- Raw logs showed payment failures.
- `metrics` rows for `payment.error_rate` were missing.
- Deployment `api:2026.06.29.1` changed parser normalization.

title: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser
text:
## Cause
The parser treated `%` as invalid and discarded the metric.

title: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser
text:
## Resolution
Rolled back the API parser release and replayed telemetry from logs.

title: Incident 014: Bad Deployment In Metrics Parser
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to payment outage, but the customer path was failing before detection noticed.

title: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes
text:
# Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes

Date: 2026-08-10 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: high
section: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes

title: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes
text:
## Summary
Payment authorization succeeded at the provider, but internal payment status writes were slow. Orders remained pending until writes completed.

title: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes
text:
## Signals
- Gateway success rate was normal.
- `payment.status_write.p95` exceeded 2s.
- Slow query logs showed missing index on idempotency lookup.

title: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes
text:
## Cause
The idempotency table grew and a lookup query lacked the expected composite index.

title: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes
text:
## Resolution
Added the missing index and replayed delayed status updates.

title: Incident 020: Payment Service Slow Database Writes
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to payment provider failures because orders stayed pending, but provider calls were healthy.

title: Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration
text:
# Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration

Date: 2026-06-02 
Service: order-service 
Severity: high

title: Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration
text:
## Summary
A new order-service version caused validation errors on coupon checkout. A direct rollback was unsafe because the release also included a forward-only migration.

title: Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration
text:
## Signals
- Errors started 6 minutes after deployment.
- Logs showed `unknown coupon_scope`.
- Database schema had already added a non-null column.

title: Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration
text:
## Cause
New validation logic rejected legacy coupon scopes.

title: Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration
text:
## Resolution
Disabled the coupon validation feature flag instead of rolling back. A patch deploy followed later.

title: Incident 010: Rollback Blocked By Migration
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to bad deployment rollback cases, but rollback was not the safe remediation.

title: Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error
text:
# Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error

Date: 2026-04-02 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: high

title: Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error
text:
## Summary
Checkout failures increased after a payment-service release. The error affected card authorization requests but did not affect saved payment method reads.

title: Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error
text:
## Signals
- `payment.error_rate` rose from 1% to 9%.
- Logs showed `missing provider_token`.
- The first error appeared 3 minutes after deployment.

title: Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error
text:
## Cause
The deployment renamed an environment variable used by the gateway client.

title: Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error
text:
## Resolution
Rolled back payment-service to the previous version and verified checkout success.

title: Incident 001: Payment Service Deployment Error
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to provider outage incidents, but rollback was correct because the provider was healthy and the failure matched deployment timing.

title: Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts
text:
# Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts

Date: 2026-06-09 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: critical

title: Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts
text:
## Summary
Payment retry fanout produced duplicate authorization attempts for a subset of checkouts. Customer charges were not captured twice, but duplicate auth alerts fired.

title: Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts
text:
## Signals
- Idempotency conflict logs increased sharply.
- Gateway timeout rate was moderate, not severe.
- Retry count rose after a client library deploy.

title: Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts
text:
## Cause
The retry wrapper regenerated idempotency keys after timeout.

title: Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts
text:
## Resolution
Rolled back the client library and paused automatic retries for affected requests.

title: Incident 011: Duplicate Payment Attempts
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to gateway timeout incidents, but idempotency conflict messages are the deciding clue.

title: Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike
text:
# Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike

Date: 2026-04-28 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: high

title: Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike
text:
## Summary
Payment attempts failed with gateway timeout errors. Order-service reported downstream payment failures, but user-service and database metrics were healthy.

title: Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike
text:
## Signals
- `payment.gateway.timeout_rate` reached 18%.
- `payment.error_rate` crossed the high severity threshold.
- Database pool usage stayed below 50%.

title: Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike
text:
## Cause
The external payment gateway had elevated latency in one region.

title: Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike
text:
## Resolution
Enabled payment degraded mode and reduced retry attempts from 3 to 1 until provider latency recovered.

title: Incident 005: Payment Gateway Timeout Spike
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Looks like payment deployment failure from the outside, but no deployment preceded the alert.

title: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency
text:
# Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency

Date: 2026-07-04 
Service: payment-service 
Severity: high
section: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency

title: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency
text:
## Summary
Payments failed quickly with provider 5xx responses. Latency stayed near baseline because failures returned immediately.

title: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency
text:
## Signals
- `payment.provider_5xx_rate` hit 12%.
- `payment.gateway.timeout_rate` stayed below 1%.
- No new payment-service deployment.

title: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency
text:
## Cause
Provider-side validation outage for card authorization.

title: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency
text:
## Resolution
Enabled alternate provider routing for eligible traffic and notified support.

title: Incident 015: Payment Provider 5xx With Healthy Latency
text:
## Retrieval Notes
Similar to gateway timeouts, but latency did not rise and 5xx rate was the primary signal.
